```{r setup, include=FALSE}
                     warning = TRUE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

The code below runs in a new R session with MIRA installed. The small
helper reads the metric-name map preserved on MIRA tables; keep its definition
when copying the later extraction examples.

```{r reader-tools}
library(MIRA)
metric_columns <- function(table, bases) {
  mapping <- attr(table, "mira_metric_names")
  actual <- bases
  mapped <- bases %in% names(mapping)
  actual[mapped] <- unname(mapping[bases[mapped]])
  stopifnot(all(actual %in% names(table)))
  actual
}
```

## Why the analysis sample matters

Read [Getting started](frequentist-long-getting-started.html) first: this
article builds on observed means and paired changes. You will audit who
contributes to each result, then distinguish missingness assumptions from
what availability tables can establish. No missing values are filled in.

An incomplete longitudinal study can have a different sample for every
question. A participant without baseline can contribute a follow-up scan measurement,
but cannot contribute a change from baseline. A participant with baseline
and final observations can contribute that change even with an intermediate
visit missing. The resulting means, paired changes, and complete-profile
tests describe different observed subsets.

This tutorial audits a synthetic observational retinal-edema follow-up
study. The outcome `cmt` is defined here as the **mean retinal thickness in
the central 1-mm-diameter OCT subfield**, in micrometres (um), often called
central subfield thickness (CST). The short variable name is a local naming
choice; it does not mean a central-point reading or interchangeably pooled
measurements from different OCT devices. The fictional study uses one
standardized instrument/segmentation protocol across visits. The
[DRCR Retina Network](https://public.jaeb.org/drcrnet/stdy/149)
uses OCT central-subfield and visual-acuity measures in retinal-edema research.
Our generated values are not trial data, diagnostic cutoffs or device norms.

Each adult contributes one study eye selected before follow-up. The record
contains its participant ID and laterality; no fellow-eye data enter this
analysis. A thickness decrease describes an anatomical change, not automatically
better vision or a clinically meaningful treatment response. BCVA is not
measured in this particular example.

Visits are scheduled at weeks 0, 2, 9 and 18, with unequal strategy groups.
These labels are hypothetical follow-up schedules, not recommended treatment
intervals. Missingness includes intermittent gaps, absent baseline scans and
final dropout generated from baseline thickness and group before some baseline
scans are masked. With fully observed baseline, that dropout component would
be compatible with MAR conditional on baseline and group. Masking baseline
too prevents extending this claim automatically to the joint pattern. The
dataset teaches availability accounting; observed outcomes cannot establish
the missingness mechanism in a real retinal study.

```{r incomplete-data}
set.seed(442031)
n <- 82L
group <- sample(c(rep("Strategy A", 50L), rep("Strategy B", 32L)))
study_eye <- sample(c("Right", "Left"), n, replace = TRUE)
person_thickness <- rnorm(n, 0, 55)
retina <- data.frame(
  participant_id = sprintf("O%03d", seq_len(n)), study_eye = study_eye,
  arm = group,
  cmt_t0 = 430 + person_thickness + rnorm(n, 0, 22),
  cmt_t2 = 410 + person_thickness + rnorm(n, 0, 25),
  cmt_t9 = 385 + person_thickness - 15 * (group == "Strategy B") + rnorm(n, 0, 28),
  cmt_t18 = 365 + person_thickness - 25 * (group == "Strategy B") + rnorm(n, 0, 30)
)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(retina$participant_id),
  all(as.matrix(retina[c("cmt_t0", "cmt_t2", "cmt_t9", "cmt_t18")]) > 0))
retina_complete <- retina  # Same people, eyes and measurements before masking.
dropout_probability <- plogis(-1.5 + 0.006 * (retina$cmt_t0 - 430) +
                               0.5 * (group == "Strategy A"))
dropout <- runif(n) < dropout_probability
retina$cmt_t18[dropout] <- NA_real_
retina$cmt_t2[sample(seq_len(n), 7)] <- NA_real_
retina$cmt_t9[sample(seq_len(n), 12)] <- NA_real_
retina$cmt_t0[c(3, 14, 29, 45)] <- NA_real_
retina$cmt_t9[8] <- Inf  # Deliberately invalid OCT export value, not a scan result.
table(retina$arm)
colSums(!is.finite(as.matrix(retina[c("cmt_t0", "cmt_t2", "cmt_t9", "cmt_t18")])))
```

The single infinite value is deliberately retained in the input to expose
the difference between raw missingness and analysis availability. It
represents a data-quality problem to investigate against the source record,
not a physiological measurement. MIRA treats `Inf` and `-Inf` as unavailable
for analysis and reports the condition. It performs no imputation.

## A simpler mechanism: independent missingness

Start with the saved complete version of these same 82 participants. We now
change only final-visit availability, using a random mask independent of all
thickness values and groups. This generator is MCAR by construction. Its realized
sample may still differ by chance; no test on observed data proves that a
real study is MCAR. The more complex `retina` dataset above remains
unchanged and is used for the rest of the article.

```{r independent-missingness}
set.seed(442032)
retina_mcar <- retina_complete
independent_mask <- runif(nrow(retina_mcar)) < 0.25
retina_mcar$cmt_t18[independent_mask] <- NA_real_
mcar_fit <- mira_info_long(
  retina_mcar, id = "participant_id", outcomes = "cmt",
  covariates = character(0), analyses = "none", verbose = FALSE
)
mcar_changes <- mcar_fit$change
mcar_endpoint <- mcar_changes[mcar_changes$from == "cmt_t0" &
  mcar_changes$to == "cmt_t18", , drop = FALSE]
kept <- !independent_mask
stopifnot(nrow(mcar_endpoint) == 1L, mcar_endpoint$n == sum(kept),
  identical(retina_mcar$participant_id, retina_complete$participant_id),
  isTRUE(all.equal(mcar_endpoint[[metric_columns(mcar_endpoint, "mean_change")]],
    mean(retina_complete$cmt_t18[kept] - retina_complete$cmt_t0[kept]))))
mcar_comparison <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("Complete-data mean change", "Observed-pair mean change",
    "Difference of observed visit means"),
  value = c(mean(retina_complete$cmt_t18 - retina_complete$cmt_t0),
    mean(retina_mcar$cmt_t18[kept] - retina_mcar$cmt_t0[kept]),
    mean(retina_mcar$cmt_t18, na.rm = TRUE) - mean(retina_mcar$cmt_t0))
)
knitr::kable(mcar_comparison, digits = 3,
  caption = "OCT central-subfield changes (um) after independent final-visit masking; the latter two quantities use different baseline samples.")
```

Only the observed-pair row describes within-person change among retained
pairs. The difference of visit means uses all baselines and fewer final
measurements. Even an independent missingness mechanism does not make those two
sample calculations algebraically identical. Neither calculation estimates
an individual causal effect.

## Fit an available-data descriptive analysis

The labels state scheduled weeks. They do not supply actual individual
visit dates, create additional measurements, or make an ordinal-time slope
a per-week rate. Irregular participant-specific visit times cannot be
encoded merely by changing display labels in this wide interface.

```{r missing-analysis}
missing_fit <- mira_info_long(
  retina, id = "participant_id", outcomes = "cmt",
  time_vars = c("cmt_t0", "cmt_t2", "cmt_t9", "cmt_t18"),
  time_labels = c("Baseline", "Week 2", "Week 9", "Week 18"),
  arm = "arm", reference_arm = "Strategy A", covariates = character(0),
  improvement_direction = "lower", stable_threshold = 25,
  analyses = c("arm_tests", "correlations"), verbose = FALSE
)
missing_fit$overview[c("n_patients", "complete_profiles", "complete_profiles_pct")]
missing_fit$diagnostics$warnings
```


The explicit `"lower"` direction and 25-um threshold provide a numerical
classification rule for this edema example only. MIRA's "Improved" label then
means a thickness reduction exceeding 25 um; it is not a validated response
definition, an OCT repeatability limit or evidence of better BCVA. The threshold
does not alter mean changes or inferential tests.

Warnings remain visible. `verbose = FALSE` prevents the large automatic
printout; it does not suppress warnings. Some checks performed inside
protected statistical modules are instead recorded on that module.
Configuration warnings and within-analysis warnings need not have identical
storage locations, so inspect both the emitted warnings and result fields.

```{r availability-tables}
knitr::kable(missing_fit$missing$by_time, digits = 1,
             caption = "Raw missing values, non-finite values, and their combined unavailability.")
desc <- missing_fit$descriptives
knitr::kable(desc[, metric_columns(desc, c(
  "label", "n", "mean", "sd", "ci_lower", "ci_upper"
))], digits = 2, col.names = c("Visit", "n", "Mean", "SD", "Lower", "Upper"),
caption = "Available OCT central-subfield thickness (um) at each scheduled visit, with pointwise 95% mean intervals.")
affected <- missing_fit$missing$by_patient$unavailable_n > 0L
head(missing_fit$missing$by_patient[affected, , drop = FALSE], 6)
stopifnot(sum(missing_fit$missing$by_time$non_finite_n) == 1,
          identical(retina$cmt_t9[8], Inf))
```

The missing-by-participant table has one row per wide input row. Its
`patient` field carries the resolved participant identifier. Descriptive
intervals still describe observed-value means; differing visit populations
can make their difference unlike the average within-participant change.

## Verify the paired and complete-profile samples

MIRA uses a separate pairwise-complete subset for each change. We can
independently count those pairs directly from the source variables.

```{r compare-samples}
changes <- missing_fit$change
expected_n <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(changes)), function(i) {
  sum(is.finite(retina[[changes$from[i]]]) &
        is.finite(retina[[changes$to[i]]]))
}, integer(1L))
stopifnot(identical(changes$n, expected_n))
expected_mean <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(changes)), function(i) {
  from <- retina[[changes$from[i]]]
  to <- retina[[changes$to[i]]]
  paired <- is.finite(from) & is.finite(to)
  mean(to[paired] - from[paired])
}, numeric(1L))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  changes[[metric_columns(changes, "mean_change")]], expected_mean)))
change_display <- changes[, metric_columns(changes, c(
  "from_label", "to_label", "n", "mean_change", "ci_lower", "ci_upper",
  "paired_t_p_adj"
))]
p_column <- metric_columns(changes, "paired_t_p_adj")
change_display[[p_column]] <- format.pval(change_display[[p_column]], digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
knitr::kable(change_display, digits = 3,
col.names = c("From", "To", "n", "Change", "Lower", "Upper", "Holm p"),
caption = "Pair-specific OCT thickness changes (um), pointwise 95% intervals and Holm-adjusted paired t tests.")
friedman <- missing_fit$advanced_tests$friedman
friedman[c("performed", "reason_skipped", "warnings", "error")]
friedman$tidy[, metric_columns(friedman$tidy, c("n", "n_timepoints", "p_raw"))]
finite_profiles <- apply(is.finite(as.matrix(retina[missing_fit$time_vars])),
                         1, all)
stopifnot(friedman$tidy$n == sum(finite_profiles))
```

Each change is later minus earlier in micrometres of central-subfield thickness; a negative
change denotes reduced thickness, without establishing functional benefit. Its interval is a pointwise Student t interval
for the mean of the observed paired differences, not an interval for a
difference between two independently observed visit means. The Holm
adjustment pools the selected visit-pair t tests within this outcome; it
does not adjust these intervals or the separate Friedman test. Independent
participants and an adequate approximation for the sampling distribution
of the mean difference remain necessary; available pairs do not repair
selection bias.

Counts alone do not identify a sample. The baseline-to-final trajectory
table lets us verify exactly which participants contribute that endpoint.
The following check also reconstructs its interval without MIRA helpers.

```{r endpoint-identities-and-interval}
endpoint_pair <- is.finite(retina$cmt_t0) &
  is.finite(retina$cmt_t18)
trajectory <- missing_fit$trajectories
trajectory_change <- trajectory[[metric_columns(trajectory, "absolute_change")]]
stopifnot(setequal(trajectory$patient[is.finite(trajectory_change)],
                   retina$participant_id[endpoint_pair]))
endpoint <- changes[changes$from == "cmt_t0" & changes$to == "cmt_t18", ,
                    drop = FALSE]
delta <- retina$cmt_t18[endpoint_pair] -
  retina$cmt_t0[endpoint_pair]
half_width <- qt(0.975, df = length(delta) - 1L) * sd(delta) / sqrt(length(delta))
expected_interval <- mean(delta) + c(-1, 1) * half_width
stopifnot(nrow(endpoint) == 1L, isTRUE(all.equal(
  as.numeric(unlist(endpoint[1L, metric_columns(endpoint, c("ci_lower", "ci_upper"))],
                    use.names = FALSE)),
  expected_interval)))
data.frame(sample = c("Enrolled", "Baseline-final pairs", "Complete profiles"),
           participants = c(nrow(retina), sum(endpoint_pair),
                            sum(finite_profiles)))
```

The Friedman test requires a complete profile at every selected visit;
its pairwise Wilcoxon follow-ups retain their own pairwise-complete
samples. The global test concerns within-participant rank differences,
whereas the paired t tests concern mean differences. A complete-profile
Friedman test is not a correction for informative dropout. Its interpretation
as evidence about all enrolled participants needs appropriate missingness
assumptions beyond the algebra of a rank test.

Correlations use pairwise-complete observations as well. Their sample-size
matrix is essential: two coefficients need not describe the same people.
Pairwise deletion can also yield a correlation matrix that is not positive
semidefinite, so do not assume it is suitable as a fitted covariance matrix.

```{r correlation-samples}
missing_fit$correlations$pairwise_n
round(missing_fit$correlations$pearson, 2)
```

The complete-profile ANOVA ICC uses only complete rows; the baseline-to-final
trajectory needs its two endpoints. Neither uses an imputed history.
Group-specific change comparisons need both endpoints and a usable arm.
Missing arm values would exclude participants from between-arm work but
would not remove their values from summaries that do not use arm.

```{r differential-availability}
arm_missing <- missing_fit$arm_analysis$missingness
missing_display <- arm_missing[, metric_columns(arm_missing, c(
  "time_label", "test", "p_value", "p_value_adj"
))]
for (column in metric_columns(arm_missing, c("p_value", "p_value_adj"))) {
  missing_display[[column]] <- format.pval(missing_display[[column]], digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
}
knitr::kable(missing_display, digits = 3, col.names = c("Visit", "Test", "p", "Holm p"),
caption = "Exploratory tests of differing unavailability by group.")
```

MIRA chooses Fisher's exact test when any expected cell count is below
five and otherwise a Pearson chi-squared test. A nonsignificant result does
not establish MCAR, equivalent missingness mechanisms, or absence of bias.
These tests have their own across-visit adjustment family.

## Change only one participant's group availability

Keep the OCT thickness measurements fixed and remove one observed group label.
Predict which denominators should change. Overall visit summaries and overall
paired changes do not need group; group-specific summaries exclude that
participant at each visit where their scan measurement is available. The selected ID
lets us audit the change without treating a missing group as a new category.

```{r missing-group-checkpoint}
missing_arm_data <- retina
masked_person <- which(endpoint_pair)[1L]
masked_id <- missing_arm_data$participant_id[masked_person]
missing_arm_data$arm[masked_person] <- NA_character_
missing_arm_fit <- mira_info_long(
  missing_arm_data, id = "participant_id", outcomes = "cmt", arm = "arm",
  time_vars = missing_fit$time_vars, time_labels = missing_fit$time_labels,
  reference_arm = "Strategy A", covariates = character(0),
  improvement_direction = "lower", stable_threshold = 25,
  analyses = c("arm_tests", "correlations"), verbose = FALSE
)
stopifnot(identical(missing_arm_fit$descriptives, missing_fit$descriptives),
  identical(missing_arm_fit$change, missing_fit$change))
group_rows <- missing_arm_fit$arm_analysis$descriptives
available_with_group <- vapply(missing_arm_fit$time_vars, function(visit) {
  sum(is.finite(missing_arm_data[[visit]]) & !is.na(missing_arm_data$arm))
}, integer(1L))
group_counts <- vapply(missing_arm_fit$time_vars, function(visit) {
  sum(group_rows$n[group_rows$time == visit])
}, integer(1L))
stopifnot(identical(unname(group_counts), unname(available_with_group)),
  masked_id %in% missing_arm_fit$trajectories$patient)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  visit = unname(missing_arm_fit$time_labels),
  all_finite_scans = missing_arm_fit$descriptives$n,
  finite_scans_with_group = unname(group_counts)),
  caption = "Group availability changes group denominators while preserving overall summaries.")
```

The warning identifies the absent group. The participant remains in the
overall result; excluding their record entirely would answer a different
question. Missing adjustment covariates similarly affect the model's rows,
as audited in [the advanced-model sample case](frequentist-long-advanced-models.html),
and do not justify inferring the model sample from descriptive counts.

## Audit adaptation and execution status

A missing number is not automatically a failed analysis. The following
audit distinguishes the evidence stored by modules; status interpretation
requires the request, reason, error, and warnings together.

| Observed state | Interpretation and next action |
|:--|:--|
| `performed = TRUE` | The module reports completed work; still inspect individual effects, samples, diagnostics, and assumptions. |
| Model disabled in `config$analyses` | Deliberately not requested; no conclusion about model feasibility. |
| `diagnostics$adaptation` records insufficient data | Requested work was disabled for an outcome before fitting. |
| `reason_skipped` names an absent package/version | Dependency unavailable; install the required version and rerun to validate it. |
| Design or effect not estimable | Data/design do not support that procedure or hypothesis; increasing software availability is insufficient. |
| Nonempty `error` or fitting warnings | Inspect the recorded failure, convergence, and numerical conditions before using output. |
| An effect has diagnostics while other effects are estimable | Output is partially usable; inspect each effect and do not extend successful inference to the failed hypothesis. |
| Procedure requires a design that is absent | Not applicable to that question; for example, an arm comparison needs at least two observed arms. |

The categories can overlap: a model can finish with warnings, and a failed
global test can leave successful pairwise tests. Do not replace every
`performed = FALSE` with a single generic label.

```{r execution-audit}
missing_fit$config$analyses
missing_fit$diagnostics$adaptation[["cmt"]]
missing_fit$advanced_tests$emmeans[c(
  "performed", "package", "reason_skipped", "error", "warnings"
)]
packages <- c("lme4", "emmeans", "afex", "geepack", "pbkrtest", "mmrm", "nparLD")
data.frame(package = packages,
           installed = vapply(packages, requireNamespace, logical(1L), quietly = TRUE))
```

Those model modules are disabled in this example, regardless of installed
software. Most analysis engines are currently declared in MIRA's `Imports`;
the implementation also guards individual engine calls. In a normal
installation their packages are installation requirements, even though
executing a particular statistical module is optional.

For an intentionally sparse OCT series, there may be too little information
even to estimate change variability. This separate diagnostic example has
only one observed value in total. The outcome remains a successful
*container* of availability information; that does not mean inference
succeeded.

```{r insufficient-information}
sparse <- data.frame(participant_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:6),
                     cmt_t0 = c(420, rep(NA_real_, 5)),
                     cmt_t1 = rep(NA_real_, 6),
                     cmt_t2 = rep(NA_real_, 6))
sparse_fit <- mira_info_long(
  sparse, id = "participant_id", outcomes = "cmt",
  covariates = character(0), analyses = c("model", "correlations"),
  verbose = FALSE
)
sparse_fit$diagnostics$adaptation[["cmt"]]
sparse_fit$advanced_tests$friedman[c("performed", "reason_skipped", "error")]
stopifnot(!sparse_fit$advanced_tests$friedman$performed,
          is.null(sparse_fit$correlations$pearson),
          is.null(sparse_fit$model$fitted_model))
```

This is insufficient information, not a plausible small-sample treatment
analysis. An unexpected outcome-level error is fatal in a single-outcome
call; in a multiple-outcome call it is isolated as a `mira_info_error_long`
element. That error class is different from the adapted successful container
above. Investigate its `error` field rather than accessing nonexistent tables.

In the current implementation, requesting plots for an outcome with no
available baseline-to-follow-up pair can raise an error while constructing
empty change-plot data. The sparse example therefore requests only model
and correlation diagnostics. Verify paired availability before requesting
plots for such an OCT series; this limitation does not indicate a successful
graphical analysis. This is a software defect to repair separately, not a
statistical requirement that every plotted participant have a complete
profile. The ordinary examples here do not depend on that defect.

## Modeling does not remove missing-data assumptions

Mixed models, GEE, and residual-correlation models use long rows complete
for outcome, participant, required arm, and retained covariates. Their
samples can differ from all the tables above. Repeated-measures ANOVA
also imposes its engine's completeness requirements. Check native model
frames and module counts when fitting them; do not infer model sample size
from `nrow(data)` or the largest descriptive count.

Likelihood-based Gaussian mixed models and MMRM can use incomplete outcome
profiles under suitable model specification and an ignorable MAR mechanism.
That is conditional on the variables actually included. Ordinary GEE with
unweighted available responses generally needs stronger response-missingness
conditions for unbiased marginal inference. MIRA's rank-longitudinal module
assumes MCAR and does not adjust for selected covariates. None of these
procedures is an automatic MNAR sensitivity analysis, and no imputation is
performed. See [advanced models](frequentist-long-advanced-models.html).

Before interpreting a study, tabulate missingness by visit and group,
investigate reasons for absent visits, verify endpoint and model samples,
and judge whether the scientific estimand survives selection into those
samples. A specialist missing-data analysis may be needed when dropout
depends on unobserved responses. Preserve those limitations alongside the
results in a [report bundle](frequentist-long-reporting.html).
